claim: A clock in the circadian field refers to an oscillator that is able to (1) free-run, (2) receive entrainment cues from the environment, and (3) compensate for changes in temperature.
source: In this context, a clock has a strict meaning, in that it refers to an oscillator that is able to (1) free-run, (2) receive entrainment cues from the environment, and (3) compensate for changes in temperature (Bell-Pedersen et al., 2005; Rosbash, 2009; Tauber et al., 2004; Young and Kay, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature in the circadian field.

claim: The emerging concept of 'autonomous clocks' adopts the word 'clock' as an umbrella term for 'timing mechanisms' without discriminating between the nomenclature of timers, hour-glass mechanisms, or different types of oscillators.
source: The emerging concept of 'autonomous clocks,' however, adopts the word 'clock' as an umbrella term for 'timing mechanisms' without discriminating between the nomenclature of timers, hour-glass mechanisms, or different types of oscillators (see Gliech and Holland, 2020 for finer details of these terminologies).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation to Gliech and Holland, 2020.

claim: In 1953, A. Howard and S.R. Pelc coined the names for different stages of a cell's division cycle: S-phase, G1, G2, and M-phases.
source: Similar to the early adoption of the words 'autonomous' and 'clock' by the circadian field, in 1953 A. Howard and S.R. Pelc have famously coined the names for different stages of a cell's division cycle – just as we know and use them today: S-phase, G1, G2, and M-phases (Howard and Pelc, 1953).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the original work by Howard and Pelc, 1953.

claim: The nomenclature of cell cycle phases was made solely based on the cycles of chromosome replication, compaction, and segregation.
source: This nomenclature, which was made solely based on the cycles of chromosome replication, compaction, and segregation, has been unintentionally extrapolated to define the temporal cycle of an entire cell.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text as a historical observation.

claim: The prevailing 'ratchet' model suggests that the principal cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk)/cyclin cell division oscillator (CCO) governs chromosome cycles.
source: With the prevailing 'ratchet' model on how the principal cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk)/cyclin cell division oscillator (CCO) may govern these chromosome cycles (Nasmyth, 1996; Stern and Nurse, 1996), such extrapolation has led to a textbook assumption that the CCO must act as a master clock to trigger and order the timing of all events in the cell (Alberts et al., 2002; Figure 1, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nasmyth, 1996 and Stern and Nurse, 1996, and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The CCO has been assumed to act as a master clock to trigger and order the timing of all events in the cell.
source: With the prevailing 'ratchet' model on how the principal cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk)/cyclin cell division oscillator (CCO) may govern these chromosome cycles (Nasmyth, 1996; Stern and Nurse, 1996), such extrapolation has led to a textbook assumption that the CCO must act as a master clock to trigger and order the timing of all events in the cell (Alberts et al., 2002; Figure 1, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alberts et al., 2002 and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The CCO may phase-lock a network of local oscillators, each of which may constitute an autonomous clock to time the cyclic execution of a specific event.
source: This paradigm has recently been under debate as to whether the CCO genuinely defines thresholds to directly trigger all these events, or alternatively, phase-locks a network of local oscillators, each of which may constitute an autonomous clock to time the cyclic execution of a specific event (Figure 1, right panel; Lu and Cross, 2010; Morgan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lu and Cross, 2010 and Morgan, 2010, and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The oscillatory release and uptake of nucleolar Cdc14 is normally coupled to cell division cycles, but can continue to operate even when the CCO is halted.
source: The 'phase-locking' hypothesis was postulated upon the observation that the oscillatory release and uptake of nucleolar Cdc14, a major phosphatase in budding yeast divisions, is normally coupled to cell division cycles, but can continue to operate even when the CCO is halted (Lu and Cross, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lu and Cross, 2010.

claim: Perturbing the CCO stops cell divisions.
source: However, since perturbing the CCO stops cell divisions, the continuous oscillations of Cdc14 did not appear to have a clear biological role.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation in the text.

claim: Evidence that autonomous Cdc14 oscillations can be phase-locked to run at the pace of cell divisions was a major step to forge a new logic on how autonomous clocks can be coordinated.
source: Although such functional redundancy in Cdc14 oscillations may have left the original observation unappreciated, evidence that autonomous Cdc14 oscillations can be phase-locked to run at the pace of cell divisions was a major step, particularly to forge a new logic on how such autonomous clocks can be coordinated more generally (Morgan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morgan, 2010.

claim: The pre-mid blastula Drosophila embryo is a powerful system to delineate principles of biological time control.
source: The past decade in biological timing research has demonstrated that the pre-mid blastula Drosophila embryo is a powerful system to delineate principles of biological time control (Aydogan et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2016), as major molecules that make up the circadian clock are not expressed until the third instar larvae stage (Yadav et al., 2014), thereby offering an opportunity to study intrinsic temporal programs in the absence of circadian cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aydogan et al., 2021 and Yuan et al., 2016.

claim: Major molecules that make up the circadian clock in Drosophila are not expressed until the third instar larvae stage.
source: The past decade in biological timing research has demonstrated that the pre-mid blastula Drosophila embryo is a powerful system to delineate principles of biological time control (Aydogan et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2016), as major molecules that make up the circadian clock are not expressed until the third instar larvae stage (Yadav et al., 2014), thereby offering an opportunity to study intrinsic temporal programs in the absence of circadian cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yadav et al., 2014.

claim: An organelle 'clock' has been demonstrated to regulate the timing of centriole formation, which is normally entrained by the cell cycle progression but can also run autonomously.
source: It is in this model system where an organelle 'clock' has recently been demonstrated to regulate the timing of centriole formation – an oscillatory mechanism that is normally entrained by the cell cycle progression, but can also run autonomously (Aydogan et al., 2020; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Centrioles are cytoskeletal organelles that form centrosomes, the major microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) that aid the assembly of mitotic spindles in dividing cells.
source: Centrioles are cytoskeletal organelles that form centrosomes – the major microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) that aid the assembly of mitotic spindles in dividing cells (reviewed in Banterle and Gönczy, 2017; Conduit et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles by Banterle and Gönczy, 2017 and Conduit et al., 2015.

claim: In most cycling systems, older centrioles (mothers) act as a platform where new centrioles (daughters) start assembling orthogonally.
source: In most cycling systems, older centrioles (i.e., the mothers) act as a platform where new centrioles (i.e., the daughters) start assembling orthogonally (Breslow and Holland, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Breslow and Holland, 2019.

claim: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4) is an enzyme essential for the formation of centrioles.
source: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4), an enzyme essential for the formation of centrioles, determines the exact site of daughter centriole assembly on the mothers (Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; and Sonnen et al., 2012.

claim: Plk4 determines the exact site of daughter centriole assembly on the mother centrioles.
source: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4), an enzyme essential for the formation of centrioles, determines the exact site of daughter centriole assembly on the mothers (Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; and Sonnen et al., 2012.

claim: Plk4 localizes to centrioles in an oscillatory manner and appears to determine an effective enzymatic threshold that initiates and times centriole biogenesis.
source: Recent work has shown that Plk4 localizes to centrioles in an oscillatory manner and appears to determine an effective enzymatic threshold that initiates and times centriole biogenesis (Aydogan et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The adaptive nature of Plk4 oscillations helps to provide homeostasis for centriole growth in fly embryos.
source: The adaptive nature of Plk4 oscillations helps to provide homeostasis for centriole growth in fly embryos (Aydogan et al., 2020; Aydogan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aydogan et al., 2020 and Aydogan et al., 2018.

claim: Plk4 oscillations persist to run even when the CCO is halted, and they continue to execute centriole formation independently of the cell cycle.
source: Remarkably, Plk4 oscillations persist to run even when the CCO is halted, and they continue to execute centriole formation independently of the cell cycle (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is illustrated in Figure 2B and is stated in the text.

claim: Oscillations of Plk4 at the centriole appear to be conserved in mammalian cells.
source: Although such oscillations of Plk4 at the centriole appear to be conserved in mammalian cells (Takao et al., 2019), functionally orthologous mechanisms may regulate the formation of MTOCs in evolutionarily distant species, such as Mps1p kinase that governs the duplication of spindle pole bodies in budding yeast (Blank et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takao et al., 2019.

claim: Mps1p kinase governs the duplication of spindle pole bodies in budding yeast.
source: Although such oscillations of Plk4 at the centriole appear to be conserved in mammalian cells (Takao et al., 2019), functionally orthologous mechanisms may regulate the formation of MTOCs in evolutionarily distant species, such as Mps1p kinase that governs the duplication of spindle pole bodies in budding yeast (Blank et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blank et al., 2020.

claim: The self-organizing nature of most mitotic spindles can waive the requirement for a functional centrosome in dividing cells.
source: In fact, the self-organizing nature of most mitotic spindles can waive the requirement for a functional centrosome in dividing cells (Basto et al., 2006; Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Heald et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Basto et al., 2006; Brugués and Needleman, 2014; and Heald et al., 1996.

claim: In the adult body where most cells are non-dividing, centriole biogenesis appears critical due to their function in templating different types of cilia.
source: In the adult body where most cells are non-dividing, however, centriole biogenesis appears critical due to their function in templating different types of cilia (Basto et al., 2006), purposed for a variety of biological roles, such as the canonical part they play in mechano-chemical signal transduction (Singla and Reiter, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Basto et al., 2006 and Singla and Reiter, 2006.

claim: Cilia play a canonical part in mechano-chemical signal transduction.
source: In the adult body where most cells are non-dividing, however, centriole biogenesis appears critical due to their function in templating different types of cilia (Basto et al., 2006), purposed for a variety of biological roles, such as the canonical part they play in mechano-chemical signal transduction (Singla and Reiter, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Singla and Reiter, 2006.

claim: Cilia are an essential component of the homeostatic program that regulates organismal health, particularly in respiratory, reproductive, and brain tissues where cells generate streams of vital fluids.
source: Cilia are an equally essential component of the homeostatic program that regulates organismal health, particularly in respiratory, reproductive, and brain tissues where cells generate streams of vital fluids (Spassky and Meunier, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spassky and Meunier, 2017.

claim: Tight regulation of centriole number is a chief determinant of cilia abundance in multi-ciliated cells.
source: As these tissues are mostly composed of multi-ciliated cells, tight regulation of centriole number is a chief determinant of cilia abundance.
evidence: The claim is stated as a logical inference from the composition of tissues.

claim: Recent work on multi-ciliated airway epithelial cells highlights the physiological importance of ciliary abundance and Plk4's potential role in the homeostatic control of centriole numbers in non-dividing cells.
source: Indeed, recent work on multi-ciliated airway epithelial cells highlights the physiological importance of ciliary abundance and Plk4's potential role in the homeostatic control of centriole numbers in these non-dividing cells (Nanjundappa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nanjundappa et al., 2019.

claim: In multi-ciliated neuron progenitors, Cdk1 is expressed at low levels that do not trigger mitosis, but is repurposed to pace certain steps of centriole biogenesis and cilia formation.
source: Similarly, another recent study has demonstrated that, in multi-ciliated neuron progenitors, Cdk1 is expressed at low levels that do not trigger mitosis, but is repurposed to pace certain steps of centriole biogenesis and cilia formation (Al Jord et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Al Jord et al., 2017.

claim: These findings collectively implicate a Cdk1-independent mechanism that drives centriole biogenesis in non-dividing cells, while regulating their numbers, at least partially, in a Plk4-dependent way.
source: These findings collectively implicate a Cdk1-independent mechanism that drives centriole biogenesis in non-dividing cells, while regulating their numbers, at least partially, in a Plk4-dependent way.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the collective findings discussed.

claim: Cytoplasmic Plk4 levels often correlate with Plk4 levels on centrioles.
source: Since cytoplasmic Plk4 levels often correlate with Plk4 levels on centrioles (Aydogan et al., 2020), an oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold (to trigger centriole biogenesis): the frequency of these integral durations may determine the number of rounds when centrioles can be produced, while the period spent above the effective enzymatic threshold may determine the size of centrioles (as depicted in Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: An oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold to trigger centriole biogenesis.
source: Since cytoplasmic Plk4 levels often correlate with Plk4 levels on centrioles (Aydogan et al., 2020), an oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold (to trigger centriole biogenesis): the frequency of these integral durations may determine the number of rounds when centrioles can be produced, while the period spent above the effective enzymatic threshold may determine the size of centrioles (as depicted in Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is stated as a speculative hypothesis based on correlations and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: In Cyanidioschyzon merolae, halting DNA replication stops the cycles of nuclei and cytokinesis, whereas chloroplast duplications continue to occur independently.
source: Intriguingly in these red algae, halting DNA replication stops the cycles of nuclei and cytokinesis, whereas chloroplast duplications continue to occur independently (Itoh et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Itoh et al., 1996.

claim: A study reports cyclic gene expression patterns during the chloroplast division cycles in C. merolae.
source: Importantly, another study (Fujiwara et al., 2009) that reports cyclic gene expression patterns during the chloroplast division cycles in C. merolae provides other candidate cyclic genes, besides PLASTID DIVISION1 and 2, with which to further investigate the molecular basis of the autonomous chloroplast division cycles.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fujiwara et al., 2009.

claim: Under lower temperatures, several events of the mitotic entry (such as nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation) occur without any detectable rise in the Cdk1 activity or cyclin B levels in early fly embryos.
source: In this work, although a large range of changes in temperature (5–22°C) did not alter the order of major mitotic events, under lower temperatures several events of the mitotic entry (such as nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation) were observed to occur without any detectable rise in the Cdk1 activity or cyclin B levels.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from the work being discussed.

claim: The segmentation clock can run independently of the cell cycle during development.
source: Until recently, studies on developmental timing have helped to reveal only a few autonomous timing mechanisms unequivocally, most notably the segmentation clock (Palmeirim et al., 1997) and the timer that controls the clonal development and differentiation of oligodendrocytes (Temple and Raff, 1986), both of whom can run independently of the cell cycle during development (Gao et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Palmeirim et al., 1997; Gao et al., 1997; and Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: The timer that controls the clonal development and differentiation of oligodendrocytes can run independently of the cell cycle during development.
source: Until recently, studies on developmental timing have helped to reveal only a few autonomous timing mechanisms unequivocally, most notably the segmentation clock (Palmeirim et al., 1997) and the timer that controls the clonal development and differentiation of oligodendrocytes (Temple and Raff, 1986), both of whom can run independently of the cell cycle during development (Gao et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Temple and Raff, 1986; Gao et al., 1997; and Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: After 14 rounds of synchronous nuclear divisions in the syncytium, thousands of nuclei rapidly become encapsulated by membrane and cellularize within the blastoderm during fly development.
source: MBT during fly development appears to be no exception: after 14 rounds of synchronous nuclear divisions in the syncytium, thousands of nuclei rapidly become encapsulated by membrane and cellularize within the blastoderm (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014.

claim: The fly embryo appears to start degrading its maternally provided RNA and simultaneously begins expressing the majority of its zygotic genes during mid-blastula transition.
source: Meanwhile, the fly embryo appears to start degrading its maternally provided RNA and simultaneously begins expressing the majority of its zygotic genes (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: The major temporal trigger of maternal-to-zygotic transition and its associated events has long been assumed to be the exponential increase in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio as a function of cell cycle progression.
source: The major temporal trigger of maternal-to-zygotic transition and its associated events – both in flies and other species – has long been assumed to be the exponential increase in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio as a function of cell cycle progression (Edgar et al., 1986; Newport and Kirschner, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edgar et al., 1986 and Newport and Kirschner, 1982.

claim: Neither the activation of zygotic genome nor the timing of cellularization is governed by an accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression in fly embryos.
source: With elegant experiments that genetically perturb the progression of cell cycle in fly embryos, recent work suggests the contrary: neither the activation of zygotic genome nor the timing of cellularization is governed by an accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression, and both events appear to occur when the nuclear divisions are halted 2–3 rounds in prior (Figure 3A; McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008; Strong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008 and Strong et al., 2020, and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Both zygotic genome activation and cellularization appear to occur when the nuclear divisions are halted 2–3 rounds in prior in fly embryos.
source: With elegant experiments that genetically perturb the progression of cell cycle in fly embryos, recent work suggests the contrary: neither the activation of zygotic genome nor the timing of cellularization is governed by an accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression, and both events appear to occur when the nuclear divisions are halted 2–3 rounds in prior (Figure 3A; McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008; Strong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008 and Strong et al., 2020, and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The timing of cellularization remains relatively similar to wild-type conditions in arrested embryos, eliminating the possibility that a mere slowing in nuclear cycles could elicit the trigger of cellularization.
source: Although the slowing of cell cycle progression (in arrested embryos) could explain the premature trigger of zygotic genome activation independently of a set N/C ratio (Strong et al., 2020), the timing of cellularization remains relatively similar to wild-type conditions, eliminating the possibility that a mere slowing in nuclear cycles could elicit the trigger of cellularization.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation that eliminates a hypothesis.

claim: These findings hint at a potential autonomous timing mechanism responsible for the onset of cellularization.
source: These findings hint at a potential autonomous timing mechanism responsible for the onset of this hallmark morphological event.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the findings discussed.

claim: Cortex contractions in the unfertilized eggs of various vertebrate and invertebrate species occur in periodic cycles that are independent of any cell cycle progression.
source: Though speculative, a potential mechanism could relate to a series of seminal observations regarding cortex contractions in the unfertilized eggs of various vertebrate and invertebrate species, occurring in periodic cycles that are independent of any cell cycle progression (Ciemerych, 1995; Hara et al., 1980; Shinagawa, 1983; Waksmundzka et al., 1984; Yoneda et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ciemerych, 1995; Hara et al., 1980; Shinagawa, 1983; Waksmundzka et al., 1984; and Yoneda et al., 1982.

claim: Cortex contractions are intimately linked to actomyosin-dependent shrinking and stretching of the embryonal membrane.
source: Just as cellularization (Schmidt and Grosshans, 2018), the cortex contractions are intimately linked to actomyosin-dependent shrinking and stretching of the embryonal membrane (Chugh and Paluch, 2018), and could potentially count a (right) number of pre-ZGA membrane cleavages that must occur prior to cellularization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt and Grosshans, 2018 and Chugh and Paluch, 2018.

claim: Previous studies have identified a series of zygotic factors that are required for the proper completion of cellularization (both structurally and temporally).
source: Indeed, previous studies have identified a series of zygotic factors that are required for the proper completion of cellularization (both structurally and temporally) (Vastenhouw et al., 2019), but to the best of our knowledge, none of these could elicit an embryonic response that can completely halt the initial trigger of cellularization.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vastenhouw et al., 2019.

claim: A recent work has revealed the molecular basis of a long-suspected developmental clock that triggers apicobasal cell polarization independently of cell cycle progression in mice embryos.
source: Although our piece particularly focuses on aspects of timing in de novo cellularization, similar questions on cell cycle autonomous timing can be proposed for other morphogenesis phenomena in early development. Indeed, a recent work has revealed the molecular basis of a long-suspected developmental clock that triggers apicobasal cell polarization independently of cell cycle progression in mice embryos (Zhu et al., 2020; Figure 3B), strongly supporting the possibility of other autonomous timing mechanisms in development and morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Metabolic regulation can be periodic and autonomously regulated.
source: Evidence that metabolic regulation can be periodic and autonomously regulated (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Slavov et al., 2011; Benjamin et al., 2005) (i.e., the metabolic cycles) had therefore opened an alternative avenue in this endeavor.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Slavov et al., 2011; and Benjamin et al., 2005.

claim: Metabolic cycles appear to be analogously conserved across species in different branches of the phylogenetic tree.
source: Recent research has demonstrated that, similar to the circadian clock (Dunlap and Loros, 2017), metabolic cycles appear to be analogously conserved across species in different branches of the phylogenetic tree; but unlike the circadian clock, the period of metabolic cycles does not appear to be set universally among different organisms (Benjamin et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Benjamin et al., 2005; and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: The period of metabolic cycles does not appear to be set universally among different organisms.
source: Recent research has demonstrated that, similar to the circadian clock (Dunlap and Loros, 2017), metabolic cycles appear to be analogously conserved across species in different branches of the phylogenetic tree; but unlike the circadian clock, the period of metabolic cycles does not appear to be set universally among different organisms (Benjamin et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benjamin et al., 2005 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Pioneering efforts in generating robust statistical methods enabled the discovery of 8 and 12 hr transcriptional rhythms in mice hepatocytes.
source: Pioneering efforts in generating robust statistical methods to study non-circadian periods with low false-discovery rates enabled the discovery of 8 and 12 hr transcriptional rhythms in mice hepatocytes (Cretenet et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010 and Hughes et al., 2009.

claim: Products of 8 or 12 hr expressing genes appear to regulate different cellular processes, from protein processing to lipid metabolism, in liver cells.
source: Products of such 8 or 12 hr expressing genes appear to regulate different cellular processes, from protein processing to lipid metabolism, in liver cells (Hughes et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hughes et al., 2009.

claim: The ~8 and ~12 hr transcriptional rhythms found in cells extracted from living mice cannot be recapitulated using their cultured counterparts.
source: Several lines of initial evidence suggested that the ~8 and ~12 hr transcriptional rhythms, which were found in cells extracted from living mice, cannot be recapitulated using their cultured counterparts, implying that they might indeed be by-products of systemic signals such as feeding cues (Cretenet et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010 and Hughes et al., 2009.

claim: Perturbing several major components in the negative arm of the circadian clock (e.g., Cry1/Cry2) demonstrates a significant dampening in the amplitude of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations.
source: Furthermore, with experiments that perturbed several major components in the negative arm of the circadian clock (e.g., Cry1/Cry2), a study demonstrated a significant dampening in the amplitude of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations, indicating that these rhythms must be generated, at least in part, by a circadian clock (and/or a feeding cue)-dependent mechanism (Cretenet et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cretenet et al., 2010.

claim: Recent studies can recapitulate the 12 hr transcriptional rhythms both in synchronized and unsynchronized hepatic cells.
source: In stark contrast to previous work, this new heave-ho that brings a methodological twist to the field can recapitulate the 12 hr transcriptional rhythms both in synchronized and unsynchronized hepatic cells – the latter eliminating confounding entrainment effects by the circadian clock (e.g., by tunicamycin incubation) or feeding cues (such as via serum deprivation).
evidence: The claim is stated as a result from recent studies using new methodological approaches.

claim: The majority of 12 hr rhythmic transcriptome in mouse liver is expressed independently of the circadian clock.
source: Importantly, this stream of work also indicates that the majority of 12 hr rhythmic transcriptome in mouse liver is expressed independently of the circadian clock (Pan et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2020 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: The biological role of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations points to the spatiotemporal control of central dogma, from gene expression to protein folding.
source: Although the biological role of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations remains unclear, current evidence – given the nature of the genes involved – points to the spatiotemporal control of central dogma, from gene expression to protein folding.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from current evidence.

claim: 12 hr transcriptional oscillations involve the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α and XBP1.
source: This particularly involves the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α (Cretenet et al., 2010), a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and XBP1 (Pan et al., 2020), the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2020; and Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: IRE1α is a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: This particularly involves the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α (Cretenet et al., 2010), a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and XBP1 (Pan et al., 2020), the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: XBP1 is the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response.
source: This particularly involves the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α (Cretenet et al., 2010), a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and XBP1 (Pan et al., 2020), the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: In 1962, Herbert Simon postulated the theory that most complex networks must take the form of hierarchy with unifying properties that are independent of their specific content.
source: In 1962, Nobel laureate Herbert Simon wrote his pioneering article The Architecture of Complexity, postulating the theory that most complex networks (from individual decision-making processes to forming societies) must take the form of hierarchy with unifying properties that are independent of their specific content (Simon, 1962).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Simon, 1962.

claim: One emergent property in most complex networks is to acquire numerous nodes that represent subdivisions and to rapidly evolve to interconnect these subunits for robustness.
source: One such 'emergent' property in most complex networks is to acquire numerous nodes that represent subdivisions and to rapidly evolve to interconnect these subunits for robustness.
evidence: The claim is stated as a general principle of complex networks.

claim: DNA replication and spindle formation are processes that can operate freely in parallel.
source: For example, although DNA replication and spindle formation are processes that can operate freely in parallel (Hartwell, 1974), they are 'latched' to occur once and only once in every cell division.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hartwell, 1974.

claim: Cycles of DNA replication can occur in the absence of nuclear divisions (e.g., the Gnu mutants in fly embryos).
source: It has been long known that cycles of DNA replication can occur in the absence of nuclear divisions (e.g., the Gnu mutants in fly embryos; Freeman et al., 1986), and recent studies on fly development argue that this phenomenon is neither unique to the embryonic tissue nor is a consequence of artificial genetic alteration: multiple rounds of DNA replication not only can occur naturally in the absence of mitosis (Zielke et al., 2011), but also can serve as part of the tissue repair program in various adult tissues (Box et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2018) – also eliminating the possibility that these autonomous cycles are just an artifact of evolution (i.e., the Darwinian requirement for the utility of intermediate forms; Darwin, 1909).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Freeman et al., 1986; Zielke et al., 2011; Box et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2018; and Darwin, 1909.

claim: Multiple rounds of DNA replication can occur naturally in the absence of mitosis.
